subject: mathematics
question_text: The sum of an infinite geometric series is 1/3 and its first term is 1/4. Find the G.P.

mark_split.label: Put the given values into S∞ = a/(1 − r)

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say which formula you rearrange, and what the question asks you to write at the end.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Put the given values into S∞ = a/(1 − r)
steps.margin_note: First mark. Substituting both given numbers into a/(1 − r) and reaching r = 1/4 earns it. Cross-multiply rather than guessing the rearrangement.
steps.memory_tip: First term divided by the sum gives 1 − r.

recall.must_convey: That 1/3 = (1/4)/(1 − r) is solved to give r = 1/4.
accept: put the sum and the first term into a over one minus r
one minus r is three fourths so r is one fourth
first term divided by the sum gives one minus r
a by one minus r lo values pettali, r one fourth vasthundi
rearrange the infinite sum formula for r

steps.why: Only one unknown is left once a and S∞ are put in, so the formula is rearranged rather than solved as two equations. Cross-multiplying gives 1 − r in one line.
common_mistakes: Writing 1 − r = (1/3) ÷ (1/4) = 4/3, which inverts the division and gives r = −1/3.
Using S∞ = a(1 − r) instead of a/(1 − r).

steps.label: Write out the terms
steps.margin_note: Second mark. At least three terms and the dots. A quick check: (1/4)/(1 − 1/4) = (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3, the sum the question gave.
steps.memory_tip: Each term is a quarter of the one before it.
lines: |r| = 1/4 < 1, so an infinite sum does exist for this ratio

recall.must_convey: That the G.P. is 1/4, 1/16, 1/64, … with each term one quarter of the previous one.
accept: the series is one fourth one sixteenth one sixty fourth and so on
multiply by one fourth each time to get the terms
the question asks for the G P not just for r
prathi term ki one fourth multiply cheyyali
check that the terms add back to one third

steps.why: The question asks for the series, not for r, so the terms have to be written out. Checking |r| < 1 confirms the ratio found is a legal one for an infinite sum.
common_mistakes: Stopping at r = 1/4 and not writing the G.P.
Writing 1/4, 2/16, 3/64 by adding a pattern instead of multiplying by r.
